title: Combination Sum
directAnswer: Find every unique combination of candidates (each reusable unlimited times) that sums to target. The canonical answer is backtracking with a start index: choose a candidate, recurse passing the SAME index `i` (so it can be reused), then un-choose. Passing `i` instead of `i+1` allows reuse; never going backwards (only `i` onward) is what prevents permutation duplicates like [2,3] and [3,2].

remember.pattern: Backtracking with a start index (choose → explore → un-choose)
remember.formula:
def backtrack(start, remaining, path):
    if remaining == 0: results.append(path[:]); return
    if remaining < 0: return
    for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
        path.append(candidates[i])
        backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i], path)  # i, not i+1 → reuse
        path.pop()                                     # un-choose
rules: Pass `i` (not `i + 1`) into the recursion so the **same** candidate can be reused unlimited times.
The loop starts at `start`, never `0` — that monotonic, never-go-backward rule is what kills permutation duplicates ([2,2,3] but never [2,3,2]).
Always `path.pop()` after the recursive call — the **un-choose** step is the discipline that keeps the path correct across sibling branches.
Append a **copy** `path[:]` to results, not `path` itself — the live list is mutated as you backtrack and would corrupt every stored answer.
Prune with `if remaining < 0: return` (or `break` if sorted) — never let a dead branch keep recursing.
whenToUse: Asked for **all** combinations / subsets that satisfy a constraint, not just a count
Elements may be reused unlimited times (or 'how many ways to make X')
The answer set must be free of permutation duplicates
Search space is a tree of choices you build incrementally
antiSignals: Only the **number** of ways is needed, not the combinations → unbounded-knapsack DP is faster
Each element used at most once and you only need a boolean → subset-sum DP
Huge candidates with tiny target → DP over target beats exponential backtracking
Order matters (permutations) → don't use a start index; track a used[] set instead
remember.takeaway: Combination Sum is the canonical 'reuse-allowed' backtracking template. The two levers — pass `i` for reuse and start the loop at `start` for dedup — recur in Combination Sum II, Subsets, Palindrome Partitioning, and Coin Change. Master choose/explore/un-choose here and the whole family falls.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can write a clean backtracking recursion and reason precisely about the two index levers — passing `i` for reuse, and starting at `start` to avoid duplicate combinations — rather than memorising a template.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Passing `i + 1` (which forbids reuse and silently fails the problem) or starting the loop at `0` (which produces permutation duplicates like [2,3] and [3,2]). Also forgetting to copy the path before storing it.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the choose/explore/un-choose template out loud, explain WHY `i` vs `i+1` controls reuse and WHY `start` controls dedup, then add sorting + early `break` pruning and give the O(N^(T/M)) bound.

problemStatement:
Given an array of **distinct** integers `candidates` and a target integer `target`, return a list of **all unique combinations** of `candidates` where the chosen numbers sum to `target`.

The **same number may be chosen from `candidates` an unlimited number of times**. Two combinations are unique if the frequency of at least one of the chosen numbers is different.

The test cases are generated such that the number of unique combinations that sum up to `target` is less than 150 for the given input.
constraints: All elements of candidates are distinct
understanding: Build every multiset of candidates that adds up to target, where each candidate may appear any number of times. We return the combinations themselves (not a count), and [2,2,3] is the same combination as [3,2,2] — order within a combination doesn't matter, so we must emit each multiset exactly once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a candidate be used more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — unlimited reuse. That's the defining feature; it's why the recursion passes `i` instead of `i + 1`.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the candidates distinct, and can they be negative or zero?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: They're distinct and all ≥ 2 (positive). Positivity matters: it guarantees the running sum is monotonic, so a branch that overshoots can be pruned immediately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of numbers within a combination matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. [2,2,3] and [2,3,2] are the same combination, so we must emit each multiset only once — handled by never letting the loop go backwards.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the input get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Tiny: target ≤ 40, candidates.length ≤ 30, and the test guarantees < 150 results. Exponential backtracking is comfortably fast enough here.

examples.explanation: 2+2+3 = 7 (2 reused twice) and 7 = 7 are the only combinations. [3,2,2] is not listed separately — it's the same multiset as [2,2,3].
Three multisets sum to 8. 2 is reused four times in the first; 3 is reused twice in the second.
The smallest candidate (2) already exceeds the target (1), so no combination is possible.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Generate Subsets, Then Filter
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to frame the search space, then immediately reject it — it can't express 'reuse' and it wastes work counting subsets that overshoot.

complexity.time: Exponential and worse — can't even bound reuse
complexity.space: O(target / min) recursion depth plus all generated lists

hints: The literal reading is 'find subsets that sum to target'. How would you enumerate every subset, then keep the ones that hit target?
A plain subset enumeration uses each element 0 or 1 times — but this problem allows unlimited reuse, so plain subsets can't even represent [2,2,3].
To allow reuse you'd have to bound a maximum copy count per candidate (target / candidate) and enumerate the cross-product — which is exactly the backtracking tree, but built blindly without pruning.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Enumerating all bounded-multiplicity combinations without pruning explores branches that have already overshot the target, doing exponential redundant work; you also generate and then discard the vast majority of partial sums.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal translation is: treat this as a subset-sum problem — enumerate combinations of candidates and keep the ones that add up to `target`. To honour reuse, you'd cap each candidate at `target / candidate` copies and enumerate the full cross-product of copy-counts, filtering at the end.

**Why this is the natural first thought.** The word 'combinations' screams 'subsets', and subset enumeration is a pattern everyone knows. It's worth saying out loud so the interviewer sees you're anchoring on a known technique before refining it.

**Why it falls apart.** Plain subset enumeration uses each element at most once, so it literally cannot produce [2,2,3] — you'd have to bolt on per-candidate multiplicity bounds, at which point you're enumerating a huge cross-product and only checking the sum at the very end. You explore branches that overshot `target` long ago, doing exponential work you could have pruned. There's no clean way to stop early. This tells the interviewer 'I know subsets' but also 'I haven't connected the reuse + pruning insight yet'.

**The fix it points to.** Instead of generating everything and filtering, *grow* the combination one choice at a time and check the running sum as you go — abandon a branch the instant it overshoots. That incremental, prunable search IS backtracking, and it makes reuse trivial: just allow re-picking the current candidate.
approaches.insight: Generate-then-filter separates 'build' from 'check'. Backtracking fuses them: you check the constraint (running sum vs target) at every node and prune dead branches immediately. That fusion is the whole reason the optimal approach is tractable.

dryRun.intro: Sketching the 'cap each candidate then cross-product' idea shows how much is wasted: most (count2, count3) pairs are checked only to be thrown away.

steps.action: max copies: 2→ up to 2, 3→ up to 1

code.python:
# Illustrative only — generate bounded multiplicities, filter at the end.
def combinationSum(self, candidates: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
    results: list[list[int]] = []

    def enumerate_counts(idx: int, path: list[int]) -> None:
        if idx == len(candidates):
            if sum(path) == target:        # check only at the leaf
                results.append(path[:])
            return
        max_copies = target // candidates[idx]   # cap reuse
        for k in range(max_copies + 1):          # try 0..max_copies copies
            enumerate_counts(idx + 1, path + [candidates[idx]] * k)

    enumerate_counts(0, [])
    return results

java.line: int maxCopies = target / c[idx];           // cap reuse for this candidate
java.explanation: We must bound reuse manually — there's no natural stop, so we cap at target/candidate copies.
The sum is checked ONLY at the leaf — every overshooting branch was explored fully before being discarded.

python.explanation: Reuse has to be bounded by hand; backtracking won't need this because it prunes on the running sum.

python.line: if sum(path) == target:        # check only at the leaf
python.explanation: Constraint checked at the very end, so overshooting branches waste full recursions.

pitfalls: Plain subset enumeration (each element 0/1 times) silently can't represent reuse — you must add multiplicity bounds.
Checking the sum only at the leaf means overshooting branches are fully explored before being thrown away.
Forgetting `new ArrayList<>(path)` / `path[:]` stores a reference to the mutating list and corrupts results.

approaches.name: Backtracking with Start Index (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'grow a combination with choose/explore/un-choose, pass i to allow reuse, start the loop at start to avoid duplicates'.
hints: Instead of generating all subsets and filtering, build one combination incrementally and abandon it the instant the running sum exceeds target. What does each recursion level decide?
At each level, loop over candidates from a `start` index and 'pick' one: add it to the path, recurse on the reduced target, then remove it (un-choose). Reuse comes from how you recurse.
To allow reusing the same number, recurse with the SAME index `i` (not `i + 1`). To avoid duplicate combinations like [2,3] and [3,2], make the loop start at `start` so you never go backwards.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Let M be the smallest candidate. The recursion tree has depth up to T/M (the longest combination), and each node branches up to N ways, giving O(N^(T/M)) nodes; copying a found combination costs O(T/M). Recursion depth (and the path) is O(T/M) extra space, excluding the output.
approaches.explanation:
Grow a combination one number at a time. Keep a running `remaining = target − (sum of path)`. At each call, loop `i` from `start` to the end: **choose** `candidates[i]` (push it), **explore** by recursing with the new remaining, then **un-choose** (pop it). When `remaining` hits 0 we record a copy of the path; when it goes negative we abandon the branch.

**Why pass `i` and not `i + 1`.** This single character is the whole 'unlimited reuse' rule. Recursing with `i` means the very next level is still allowed to pick `candidates[i]` again, so 2 can be chosen as many times as the budget allows ([2,2,2,2]). If you passed `i + 1` you'd forbid reuse and you'd be solving Combination Sum II (each element once) instead. Say this trade-off out loud — interviewers love seeing you know exactly which line controls which behaviour.

**Why the loop starts at `start`, never at 0.** This is the dedup lever. By only ever moving forward (or staying put), we enforce that every combination is generated in non-decreasing index order. So we'll build [2,3] but never [3,2], because once we've moved past index 0 we can't pick 2 again at a later level. That monotonic discipline is precisely what makes the output a set of *combinations* (multisets) rather than *permutations* — without it you'd emit [2,3] and [3,2] as separate answers.

**Why the un-choose (pop) is non-negotiable.** `path` is a single shared list reused across the entire tree. After exploring the branch where we picked `candidates[i]`, we must `pop()` it so the next sibling iteration starts from the correct prefix. Skip the pop and the path bleeds choices across branches, producing garbage. And when we hit a solution we append `path[:]` (a *copy*) — appending the live list stores a reference that later pops will mutate.
approaches.insight: The two index levers are independent knobs: **passing `i` vs `i+1`** controls reuse (unlimited vs once), and **the loop's start position** controls ordering (combinations vs permutations). Almost every problem in the subsets/combinations family is just a different setting of these two knobs — internalise them and you stop memorising templates.

code.python:
def combinationSum(self, candidates: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
    results: list[list[int]] = []
    candidates.sort()                        # enables the early break prune

    def backtrack(start: int, remaining: int, path: list[int]) -> None:
        if remaining == 0:
            results.append(path[:])          # store a COPY of the path
            return
        for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
            if candidates[i] > remaining:    # sorted → no later candidate fits
                break
            path.append(candidates[i])       # choose
            backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i], path)  # explore, i = reuse
            path.pop()                       # un-choose

    backtrack(0, target, [])
    return results

java.line: Arrays.sort(candidates);                 // enables the early break prune
java.explanation: Sorting lets us break the loop as soon as one candidate overshoots — every later one is bigger.

java.line: results.add(new ArrayList<>(path));  // store a COPY of the path
java.explanation: Append a copy; the live `path` keeps mutating as we backtrack and would corrupt stored answers.

java.line: for (int i = start; i < candidates.length; i++) {
java.explanation: Loop starts at `start`, never 0 — never going backward is what prevents permutation duplicates.

java.line: if (candidates[i] > remaining) break;   // sorted → no later candidate fits
java.explanation: Pruning: since sorted, if this one overshoots, all later ones do too — stop the whole loop.
The CHOOSE step of the backtracking template.

java.line: backtrack(candidates, i, remaining - candidates[i], path, results); // explore, i = reuse
java.explanation: Pass `i` (not i+1) so the same candidate can be reused; reduce remaining as we go.
The UN-CHOOSE step — restore the path so the next sibling branch starts clean.

python.line: candidates.sort()                        # enables the early break prune
python.explanation: Sorting makes the `break` valid: once a candidate overshoots, all later ones do too.

python.line: results.append(path[:])          # store a COPY of the path
python.explanation: `path[:]` snapshots the list; appending `path` itself stores a reference that later pops mutate.
Start at `start`, not 0 — the monotonic, never-backward rule prevents [2,3]/[3,2] duplicates.

python.line: if candidates[i] > remaining:    # sorted → no later candidate fits
python.explanation: Prune the branch: sorted order means no subsequent candidate can fit either.

python.line: backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i], path)  # explore, i = reuse
python.explanation: EXPLORE with `i` so the candidate stays available for reuse on the next level.
UN-CHOOSE: pop it back off so the sibling iteration sees the original prefix.

edgeCases.behavior: Sorted, loop picks 2 but 2 > remaining(1) → break immediately, remaining never reaches 0 → returns []. The prune handles it in O(1).
Builds [2,2,2,2], [2,3,3], [3,5] in non-decreasing index order; never emits [3,3,2] or [5,3] because the loop only moves forward.

pitfalls: Passing `i + 1` instead of `i` — forbids reuse and solves the wrong problem (Combination Sum II).
Starting the loop at 0 instead of `start` — produces permutation duplicates like [2,3] and [3,2].
Appending `path` instead of `path[:]` / `new ArrayList<>(path)` — every stored answer ends up mutated to the same final state.

commonMistakes: Passing `i + 1` into the recursion, which forbids reuse and silently solves a different problem.
Starting the inner loop at 0 instead of `start`, producing duplicate combinations like [2,3] and [3,2].
Storing the live `path` reference instead of a copy, so every result mutates to the same final list.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Passing i + 1 (kills reuse)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Recursing with `i + 1` forbids re-picking the current candidate, so [2,2,3] can never form. That's Combination Sum II's rule, not this problem's.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
    path.append(candidates[i])
    backtrack(i + 1, remaining - candidates[i], path)  # no reuse!
    path.pop()
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
    path.append(candidates[i])
    backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i], path)      # reuse allowed
    path.pop()

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Looping from 0 (permutation duplicates)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Starting at 0 lets later levels pick earlier candidates again, so you emit both [2,3] and [3,2]. Starting at `start` enforces non-decreasing order and dedups.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(0, len(candidates)):          # always from 0
    path.append(candidates[i])
    backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i], path)
    path.pop()
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(start, len(candidates)):      # from start
    path.append(candidates[i])
    backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i], path)
    path.pop()

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Storing the live path reference
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `results.append(path)` stores the same list object; subsequent pops mutate it, so all results end up identical (often empty). Append a snapshot.

followupVariations.title: Combination Sum II
followupVariations.hint: Each number used once → pass `i + 1`; candidates have duplicates → sort and skip `candidates[i] == candidates[i-1]` at the same level.

followupVariations.title: Combination Sum III
followupVariations.hint: Use digits 1–9, each once, exactly k numbers → pass `i + 1` and add a path-length check alongside the sum check.

followupVariations.title: Combination Sum IV
followupVariations.hint: Order matters and only the COUNT is needed → switch to DP over target (unbounded, permutations); backtracking would TLE.

followupVariations.title: Subsets
followupVariations.hint: Same start-index template, but record the path at every node instead of only when a sum target is hit.

patternNote: Canonical Backtracking with a Start Index (choose → explore → un-choose). Recognise it whenever you must enumerate ALL combinations/subsets under a constraint. The two levers — pass `i` for reuse, start the loop at `start` for dedup — also drive Combination Sum II, Subsets, Permutations, and Palindrome Partitioning.
